name: ScramDB
license: Proprietary, closed source; free single-node Community edition capped at 64 GiB, Enterprise licence key required for clustering; no published licence agreement found
summary: A brand-new, closed-source database that speaks the PostgreSQL protocol and promises transactions, analytics and vector search on one copy of the data; first builds shipped in summer 2026.
intro: ScramDB ships as one binary for Linux (x86-64 with AVX2, or arm64), a Docker image and a Helm chart. A node listens on port 5432 for the PostgreSQL wire protocol, serves Prometheus metrics and a health check on 9090, and runs an MCP server for AI agents on 9191. Its storage engine, Tundra, keeps one columnar copy of each table: writes land in a write-optimized area and are visible immediately, then get folded into compressed column blocks with per-block min/max summaries so scans can skip data. A write-ahead log handles crash recovery, and MVCC gives isolation up to serializable. Queries are compiled to native code in the background and the compiled code is cached on disk; heavy queries over at least 50,000 rows can be offloaded to an NVIDIA, AMD or Apple GPU, falling back to the CPU. Functions run as sandboxed packages, and the install includes packages for BM25 text scoring, embeddings, H3 cells, HyperLogLog and other sketches. `CREATE DATABASE ... CLONE` makes an instant copy-on-write branch, and with WAL archiving to S3, GCS or Azure a branch can start from a past timestamp.

It is very new. Its author, Theo M. Bulut, announced the first version on 23 July 2026. The installer pulls automated prerelease builds named after git commits from a GitHub releases repository (the latest from 30 September 2026); Docker Hub has a `1.0.0` image tag from 18 September, but the installer’s index lists no stable version yet. The source is not public, and the site has no terms or licence page. The Community edition is free on a single node and turns read-only past 64 GiB of data. Enterprise, priced on request, lifts the cap and unlocks clustering: a node with a `[cluster]` section in its config refuses to start without an Enterprise or Trial key, and a key only covers binaries built before its end date. There is no managed service.
strengths: Quick to try: a one-line installer or `docker run`, then any PostgreSQL driver, `psql` or BI tool connects
Branching and point-in-time recovery are built in: copy-on-write `CLONE`, branches from a past timestamp, and WAL archiving switched on in the Docker image
Search, vector, geospatial and sketch functions come as bundled sandboxed packages, with no C extensions to compile
Unusually candid docs: a limitations page lists what doesn’t work yet with workarounds, and the licensing page spells out exactly what is enforced
limits: Pre-release in practice, from a tiny vendor: first announced in July 2026, the installer still serves untagged prerelease builds, and every blog post is by its author; there are no published customers or independent reviews
Closed source with no published licence terms; clustering, the core of the “distributed hyperscale” pitch, needs an Enterprise key at an unpublished price, and Community stops writes at 64 GiB

Performance claims are self-reported: its benchmark page sets ScramDB’s own single-node run against other systems’ published results, and ClickBench’s maintainer removed the “UTAP” and “JIT” tags from its entry, calling them made up

Gaps listed in its own docs: backups are cold (the server must be stopped), single-row write latency is still being tuned, and there are no range types, XML, locale collations, function overloading or incremental materialized view refresh
The Docker image starts with authentication disabled on all interfaces, and the site contradicts itself in places, for example calling MCP “on the roadmap” while the docs describe an MCP server

values: Ships and is documented; compatibility is self-tested

rows.label: Single-node install
values: Ships for Linux x86-64 and arm64, Docker and Helm; no native macOS build

rows.label: Multi-node and multi-region clusters
values: Documented, but needs an Enterprise or Trial key; no independent reports found

rows.label: Backups and recovery
values: Cold base backups, WAL archiving, point-in-time recovery and branching; no online backup

rows.label: GPU execution

story: ScramDB is the work of Theo M. Bulut. In his launch post he writes that he started eight years earlier, when analytical systems were still built around traditional execution models, and set out to build one system that would make Redis, PostgreSQL, CDC tools, Kafka, vector databases and search engines unnecessary for most teams. The project went through what he calls multiple burnouts on the way.

The ScramDB Labs GitHub organisation, which gives Germany as its location, dates from 2020 and holds earlier open-source pieces from the same work: Callysto, a stream processing framework (2021, Apache 2.0), and a white paper on ANODE, an on-disk approximate nearest-neighbour index (2024). The database itself stayed closed. A Docker Hub repository appeared in March 2026, and on 23 July 2026 Bulut announced the first version.

Automated builds have been published to GitHub since August 2026, ClickBench results were submitted in September, and a `1.0.0` image tag followed on Docker Hub. It is too early to say what, if anything, it has changed.

choices.choice: One columnar copy with a write-optimized area
choices.why: Running a row store for transactions and a column store for analytics means a pipeline between them and stale dashboards. Tundra takes writes into a fast area and folds them into compressed columns in the background, so both workloads read the same data.

choices.choice: The PostgreSQL wire protocol instead of a new API
choices.why: So existing drivers, ORMs and BI tools connect as they are, with no ScramDB SDK to learn.
PostgreSQL loads untrusted C extensions into the server, where one bug can crash it. ScramDB functions run in a sandbox and get only the access their package declares.

choices.choice: A free single node, a licence key for clustering
choices.why: Anyone can run the full engine on one machine, while running many nodes, which is what the company sells, needs an Enterprise licence enforced at startup.

timeline.text: Theo M. Bulut starts work on the engine, by his own account

First version announced on 23 July; prerelease builds from August
